North India
North
Rivers, ruins and *marble* at dawn.
The India of the great rivers and the great empires: Mughal Delhi and Agra, the ghats of Varanasi, the Ganges at Rishikesh and the Golden Temple at Amritsar.

North India is where many first journeys begin, and for good reason. Delhi holds seven historic cities inside one modern capital, from the red sandstone of Humayun's Tomb to the lanes of Old Delhi, where a cycle rickshaw can carry you past spice wholesalers, silversmiths and a seventeenth-century mosque in the space of ten minutes.

Follow the plains east and the story deepens. In Agra, the Taj Mahal changes color with the hour, pale gray before sunrise, warm white at noon, rose at dusk. In Varanasi, the oldest living city on the Ganges, pilgrims bathe at first light and evening aarti fills the river with lamps, bells and the smell of camphor and marigold.

Further north the land rises. Rishikesh sits where the Ganges leaves the Himalayan foothills, a town of ashrams, suspension bridges and clear green water. Amritsar, in the Punjab, is home to the Golden Temple, whose community kitchen serves free meals to tens of thousands of people every day, cooked and served by volunteers. We plan the pace so each place has room to breathe.

Is the Taj Mahal open every day?

The Taj Mahal is closed to general visitors on Fridays, when it is reserved for prayers. It opens around sunrise on other days, and we build your Agra stay around the best light. Opening rules occasionally change, so we confirm them when we book.
How much time should we spend in Varanasi?

Two nights is the minimum we recommend, which gives you an evening aarti, a dawn boat ride and time in the old city. Three nights lets you add Sarnath, where the Buddha gave his first sermon, and a slower look at the weaving workshops.
What is the fog like in winter?

In December and January, dense morning fog can settle over the northern plains and delay flights and trains. We build in buffer time, favor later departures and use road transfers where it makes sense. Days usually clear into crisp sunshine.

Rajasthan
Palaces, forts and *desert* light.
The land of the Rajput kingdoms: hilltop forts, lake palaces and blue and golden cities strung across the Thar Desert.

Rajasthan was once a patchwork of princely states, each with its own ruling family, its own fort and its own fierce pride. That history is still close to the surface. Many palaces are now hotels run by descendants of the families who built them, and a conversation over tea on a haveli rooftop can easily turn into three centuries of family stories.

Each city has its own color and character. Jaipur is pink and busy, a planned city of bazaars and the honeycombed Hawa Mahal. Udaipur is white and serene, its palaces reflected in Lake Pichola. Jodhpur sprawls in indigo beneath Mehrangarh, one of the most imposing forts in India, and Jaisalmer rises from the sand in honey-colored stone.

Between the cities is a quieter Rajasthan we love just as much: village markets, stepwells, block-printing workshops and dunes where you can watch the sun go down with nothing but the sound of camel bells. Pushkar, with its holy lake and ghats, is a gentle pause on the way. We balance the grand set pieces with these slower, more personal moments.

How many days do we need in Rajasthan?

Ten to twelve days lets you see Jaipur, Jodhpur, Udaipur and either Jaisalmer or Pushkar without rushing. With a week, we would focus on two or three cities and add a rural stay rather than racing between forts.
Can we really stay in palaces?

Yes. Rajasthan has many heritage hotels in former palaces, forts and havelis, from grand lakeside properties to intimate family homes. We know the owners and managers personally and match the stay to your taste and budget.
Is it too hot to visit in April?

April is warm, often well into the high thirties Celsius by afternoon. It can work with early starts, long lunches and a pool, and prices are softer. From May the heat becomes oppressive for sightseeing, so we usually suggest the hills instead.

South India
South
Backwaters, temples and *spice* air.
A greener, slower India of palm-lined backwaters, towering temple gateways, tea and spice hills and the beaches of Goa.

South India runs on a different rhythm. In Kerala, life follows the water: rice barges converted into houseboats drift along the backwaters, past village churches, toddy shops and women washing brass pots at the water's edge. Up in the Western Ghats, the air smells of cardamom and wet earth, and tea estates roll across the hills around Munnar.

Tamil Nadu is the great temple country. At Madurai, the gopurams of the Meenakshi Temple are crowded with thousands of painted figures, and evening ceremonies carry on much as they have for centuries. Along the coast, the French quarter of Pondicherry offers mustard-yellow villas and bakeries, and Chettinad's mansions serve one of India's great regional cuisines.

Karnataka holds the royal splendor of Mysore and the boulder-strewn ruins of Hampi, once the capital of the Vijayanagara empire. And Goa, with its Portuguese churches, spice farms and long beaches, is the place to slow right down at the end of a journey. We stitch these together by road, rail and short flights so the south feels unhurried.

Is the monsoon a bad time to visit Kerala?

Not at all, if you choose it for the right reasons. From June to August the landscape is at its greenest, prices are lower and Ayurvedic practitioners consider it the ideal season for treatment. Expect heavy downpours with bright spells, and fewer beach days.
Should we book a shared or private houseboat?

We almost always recommend a private houseboat with your own crew. We choose operators who keep their boats well maintained, cook fresh local food and are willing to take quieter routes away from the busiest stretches near Alleppey.
Can we combine Kerala with Tamil Nadu?

Yes, and it makes a wonderful journey. A common route crosses the Western Ghats from Kerala's tea hills to Madurai, then continues to Chettinad and the coast. Two weeks gives you time for both without long days on the road.

The Himalaya
Himalaya
High passes and *prayer* flags.
India's mountain north: the high desert of Ladakh, the valleys of Himachal Pradesh and the tea gardens and monasteries of Darjeeling and Sikkim.

The Indian Himalaya is not one place but many. Ladakh is a high-altitude desert of ochre mountains, turquoise rivers and whitewashed monasteries clinging to rock. Life here has a Tibetan Buddhist rhythm: butter lamps, prayer wheels, apricot orchards in summer and a hospitality that feels completely unforced. Summer days are bright and dry, nights are cool, and the light is so clear that distant peaks look close enough to touch.

Himachal Pradesh is greener and gentler. Old colonial hill stations such as Shimla give way to deodar forests, apple orchards and Kangra Valley villages, while Dharamshala and McLeod Ganj are home to the Tibetan community in exile. Further up, the Spiti Valley offers some of the most dramatic road journeys in the country, past cliff-top gompas and villages of mud-brick houses stacked against the slopes.

In the east, Darjeeling looks across its tea estates to Kangchenjunga, the world's third-highest mountain, and the toy train still puffs up from the plains. Neighbouring Sikkim is small, green and devoutly Buddhist, with monasteries, rhododendron forests and walks through villages where every house seems to have a garden. Whatever you choose, we plan carefully for altitude and access.

Will altitude be a problem in Ladakh?

Leh sits at around 3,500 meters, so acclimatization matters. We plan two or three gentle days on arrival before any higher excursions and choose routes that climb gradually. If you have any medical concerns, speak to your doctor before traveling.
Do we need permits for the Himalaya?

Some areas, including parts of Ladakh and Sikkim near international borders, require permits for visitors, and rules differ for Indian and foreign nationals. We arrange these for you, and we check the current requirements each season because they do change.
Can we visit the mountains in winter?

Ladakh in winter is very cold and many roads and passes are closed, though it suits specialist trips such as snow leopard tracking. Lower hill stations like Shimla and Darjeeling can be crisp and clear in winter, but some high-altitude areas will be out of reach.

Central India
Tiger country, quietly *wild*.
The forested heart of India and its great tiger reserves: Ranthambore, Bandhavgarh, Kanha and Tadoba.

Central India is the country of The Jungle Book, a landscape of sal and teak forest, bamboo thickets, grassy meadows and rocky outcrops. It is also one of the best places in the world to see a wild tiger. Early mornings begin with a jeep, a naturalist and a thermos of chai, listening for the alarm calls of spotted deer and langur monkeys.

Each reserve has its own character. Ranthambore has ruined pavilions and a thousand-year-old fort inside the park. Bandhavgarh is known for a high density of tigers. Kanha's meadows are home to the hard-ground barasingha, a deer brought back from the edge of extinction. Tadoba, in Maharashtra, has become one of the most reliable parks for sightings in recent years.

Wildlife is never guaranteed, and we never pretend it is. What we can promise is the right lodges, experienced naturalists and safari permits secured early. We favor lodges that employ local people, support conservation and take the forest seriously, and we combine the parks with temples such as Khajuraho for a fuller picture of the region.

Will we definitely see a tiger?

No one can guarantee a wild tiger, and we would be wary of anyone who does. With three or four nights and six to eight drives in a good reserve, many of our travelers do see one. We build in enough drives to give you a fair chance and plenty more to enjoy.
When are the parks closed?

Core zones of most central Indian reserves close during the monsoon, typically from around July to September, and many parks have a weekly closure for some drives. Buffer zones may stay open. Dates are set by the forest departments and change, so we check each season.
How far in advance do we need safari permits?

Permits for popular zones can sell out months ahead, especially from October to May. Booking early lets us secure the best zones and timings, and our lodges help us plan drives around current sightings.

East & Northeast
Where India's *frontier* begins.
The literary, food-loving city of Kolkata and the green hills, rivers and tribal cultures of Meghalaya, Assam and Nagaland.

Kolkata is a city of ideas and appetites. Grand colonial buildings such as the Victoria Memorial stand beside crumbling mansions, flower markets under the Howrah Bridge and coffee houses where poets and students have argued for a century. Bengali food alone, with its mustard-oil fish curries and sweets made from fresh cheese, is reason enough to come.

Beyond lies the Northeast, a region of seven states that many travelers never reach. Meghalaya, the abode of clouds, has living root bridges grown by Khasi villagers from the roots of rubber fig trees. Assam is a land of tea gardens and the Brahmaputra, where Kaziranga National Park shelters the majority of the world's greater one-horned rhinos.

Nagaland, in the far east, is home to many distinct Naga tribes with their own languages, crafts and festivals, best known to visitors through the Hornbill Festival each December. Travel here is slower and simpler than in the rest of India, which is exactly the appeal. We work with small local operators and homestays who open doors that would otherwise stay closed.

Is the Northeast suitable for a first trip to India?

Andaman Islands
Islands
Clear water, slow *island* days.
A remote archipelago in the Bay of Bengal with white-sand beaches, coral reefs and rainforest, made for unwinding at the end of a journey.

The Andaman Islands lie far out in the Bay of Bengal, closer to Myanmar than to mainland India. Only a handful of the islands are open to visitors, and that is part of their charm: rainforest runs down to the sand, the water is a startling turquoise and the pace of life is governed by ferry timetables and the tides.

Port Blair, the capital, is the gateway, home to the Cellular Jail, a sobering memorial to India's freedom struggle. From there, ferries cross to Swaraj Dweep, still widely known as Havelock, with its long, quiet beaches, and to smaller Shaheed Dweep (Neil Island), where cycling between villages and coconut groves is the main event.

Beneath the surface are coral reefs, turtles and shoals of reef fish, with good snorkelling and diving for beginners and the experienced alike. We pair the islands with the mainland as a restful finale, choosing small beach resorts with care, and advise on responsible snorkelling and the protected status of the islands' indigenous communities.

How do we get to the Andaman Islands?

Flights connect Port Blair with major mainland cities including Chennai, Kolkata and Delhi. From Port Blair, government and private ferries cross to Havelock and Neil. We book everything in sequence so connections are realistic.
Are the Andamans good for diving beginners?

Yes. Havelock in particular has well-run dive centers offering introductory dives and courses in calm, clear water. We recommend operators with strong safety records who respect the reefs and keep group sizes small.
How many nights should we spend in the islands?

Four to six nights works well, usually split between Havelock and either Neil Island or a night in Port Blair. Because ferries and weather can occasionally disrupt plans, we avoid tight connections on your final day.

Mughal marble, pink *Jaipur* and the old lanes of Delhi.
India's classic first journey, told properly: Old Delhi's spice lanes, the Taj Mahal at first light and Jaipur's forts and bazaars, with time to breathe between them.

Delhi, Agra and Jaipur sit a few hours apart, which is why the Golden Triangle is so often rushed. We slow it down. You'll walk Old Delhi with someone who grew up in its lanes, reach the Taj Mahal as the gates open and the marble turns from gray to rose, and give Jaipur three full days rather than an afternoon.

Between the headline monuments come the moments that make the trip yours: a breakfast of nihari near Jama Masjid, the vast stepped geometry of Chand Baori at Abhaneri, a morning with block printers in Sanganer, and an evening on a haveli rooftop as the city's temples ring out below.

It works beautifully as a first taste of India or as the opening chapter of a longer journey. Ask your specialist about adding two nights in Ranthambore for tiger safaris, or continuing on to Udaipur and the lakes.

Tigers & Temples
Sal forests, sacred rivers and the *tiger*.
Varanasi's ghats and Khajuraho's carved temples, then deep into the sal forests of Bandhavgarh and Kanha in search of the Bengal tiger, with naturalists who know every track.

This is a journey through the heart of India, where ancient faith and wild forest sit side by side. Begin on the Ganges at Varanasi, among the oldest living cities on earth, then travel to Khajuraho, whose thousand-year-old Chandela temples are carved with some of the finest sculpture in India.

From there, the forests of Madhya Pradesh take over. Bandhavgarh has one of the highest densities of tigers in India, set around a ruined hilltop fort and a tenth-century reclining Vishnu. Kanha is vaster and wilder, with sal forests and open meadows where herds of barasingha, the rare hard-ground swamp deer, graze at dawn.

You'll take around eight jeep safaris with expert naturalists who read the forest by alarm calls and pugmarks. Tigers are never guaranteed, but your odds here are as good as anywhere in the world, and the leopards, sloth bears, wild dogs and birdlife are rewards of their own.

Ladakh feels like the roof of the world, because it nearly is. Leh sits at around 3,500 meters, ringed by snow peaks and barley fields, and the journey begins with the most important thing at altitude: rest. Three easy days in Leh let your body adjust while you explore the old town, the palace and the great monasteries of the Indus Valley.

Then the road climbs over the Khardung La, one of the highest motorable passes in the world, and drops into the Nubra Valley, where Bactrian camels wander sand dunes beneath glaciers. From Nubra, follow the Shyok River to Pangong Tso, a long lake that changes from turquoise to deep cobalt as clouds pass overhead.

Nights are spent in warm, family-run places: a Ladakhi homestay in Nubra, a comfortable camp by the lake, and a quiet hotel in Leh. Days are full of butter tea, monastery chants, apricot orchards and the sort of silence that stays with you long after.

In Varanasi, you'll see the city's rituals from a rowing boat at dawn and dusk, walk its lanes with a scholar who has spent a lifetime here, and visit Sarnath, where the Buddha first taught. In Rishikesh, there's time to slow right down: yoga and meditation sessions by the Ganges, quiet walks in the foothills and evening aarti at Parmarth Niketan.

We arrange each experience with care, from respectful behavior at the burning ghats to the right way to cover your head at a gurdwara. Ask your specialist about adding two nights in Bodh Gaya, where the Buddha attained enlightenment, an easy drive from Varanasi.

India has many cuisines, not one, and the best way to understand them is to eat your way across the country with people who grew up at its tables. This journey travels from north to east to south, each stop a different chapter: Mughal, Punjabi, Awadhi, Bengali and Chettinad.

In Delhi, you'll eat parathas and nihari in the lanes behind Jama Masjid. In Amritsar, you'll help roll chapatis in the world's largest free kitchen, then hunt down buttery kulchas. Lucknow brings the melt-in-the-mouth galouti kebab, invented for a toothless nawab; Kolkata, phuchka on the street, Chinese breakfast in Tiretta Bazaar and mishti doi.

The journey ends in Chettinad in Tamil Nadu, where merchant families built grand mansions with Burmese teak and Italian marble, and where a fiery, fragrant cuisine of black stone flower, star anise and dried chillies is served on banana leaves. Along the way: markets at dawn, home kitchens and cooking classes.

Pugmarks in the *dust* at first light.
Dawn drives through the sal and bamboo forests of central India and Rajasthan with naturalists who read the jungle like a newspaper.

The gates open at sunrise and the open jeeps roll in single file, engines low. For the first hour you listen more than you look: the alarm bark of a chital, the sharp call of a langur from the canopy, the sudden silence that means something large is moving. Your naturalist will stop, kill the engine and point to a fresh pugmark pressed into the track, still crisp at the edges.

India is home to roughly three-quarters of the world's wild tigers, and parks such as Kanha, Bandhavgarh, Pench, Tadoba and Ranthambore give some of the finest chances anywhere to see one. But a good safari is never only about the tiger. Kanha's meadows hold the hard-ground barasingha, a swamp deer brought back from the edge of extinction. Ranthambore's forest runs right up to the walls of a tenth-century fort. There are sloth bears, gaur, jungle cats, and more than two hundred species of birds.

We plan two to four nights per park so you have several drives across different zones, which matters far more than luck. We choose lodges that employ and train people from neighbouring villages, and we match you with naturalists who care as much about the crested serpent eagle on the branch as the big cat in the grass.

Ganges evening aarti

Watch the nightly Ganga aarti from a wooden boat on the river at Varanasi, with a guide who explains each gesture.

As the sun drops behind the city, young priests in saffron and gold take their places on raised platforms at Dashashwamedh Ghat. Conch shells sound. Bells ring. Then the great brass lamps, tiered and blazing, are lifted and swung in slow arcs toward the river as the crowd chants with them.

Varanasi is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world and among Hinduism's holiest places. The aarti, an offering of light to the goddess Ganga, is performed every evening. From a boat just off the steps you see the whole scene at once: the flames, the clouds of incense, the faces lit gold, and small leaf-cup diyas floating past you downstream.

Your guide will explain what you are seeing and why it matters, and the next morning we suggest a sunrise boat ride, when the ghats belong to bathers, washermen, yoga and quiet prayer. Rishikesh and Haridwar hold their own evening aartis, smaller and closer to the mountains.

India's best-loved festival, when homes, temples and whole cities glow with oil lamps, and families gather for sweets, prayers and fireworks.

Do I need a visa to visit India?

Most visitors need a visa. Citizens of many countries, including the UK, US, Canada, Australia and much of Europe, can apply online for an e-Visa, which is usually the simplest option for tourism. Apply only through the official Indian government website, and allow plenty of time before you travel.

Your passport should normally be valid for at least six months from your arrival date, with at least two blank pages. Some e-Visa types allow single or multiple entries and have different lengths of stay, so check which suits your plans.
Your specialist will remind you when to apply and can talk you through the process, but the application must be made by you, and the final decision rests with the Indian authorities.
Verify against official Indian government sources (indianvisaonline.gov.in) before travel; rules change.
When is the best time to visit India?

India is so large that there is always somewhere wonderful to go. For most of the country, including Rajasthan, the Golden Triangle and Kerala, the classic season runs from October to March, when days are warm, dry and sunny.

The Himalaya works the other way round: Ladakh is best from June to September, and Sikkim and Darjeeling shine in spring and autumn. Central India's tiger reserves are open from October to June, with the best sightings often from February to May as the forest thins and animals come to water.
April to June can be very hot across the northern plains, so we lean toward the mountains, the hills or shorter, early-start days in that period.
Is it worth traveling during the monsoon?

Yes, with the right plan. The southwest monsoon generally reaches Kerala in early June and spreads north through July, bringing a landscape of vivid green, fewer visitors and often lower prices. Rain often comes in heavy bursts rather than all day.

The monsoon is a traditional season for Ayurveda in Kerala, and Udaipur's lakes are at their most beautiful afterwards. Ladakh and Spiti lie in the Himalayan rain shadow and are at their best during these months.
Most tiger reserves' core zones close from July to September, and some roads, beaches and hill areas can be affected by flooding or landslides. We plan around this and build in flexibility.
What vaccinations and health precautions do I need?

See your doctor or a travel clinic six to eight weeks before you travel. Commonly recommended vaccinations for India include hepatitis A and typhoid, with others such as hepatitis B, rabies or Japanese encephalitis depending on your plans. Make sure routine vaccinations are up to date.
Malaria and dengue are present in parts of India. Ask your doctor whether you need antimalarial medication for your route, and use insect repellent, especially at dawn and dusk.
Pack any prescription medication in its original packaging, with a copy of your prescription, and bring a small kit for stomach upsets. Good hospitals are found in all major cities.
Check with your doctor or a travel clinic and your government's travel health guidance.
Is the food and water safe?

Indian food is one of the great joys of a trip, and with sensible care most travelers eat brilliantly without problems. Drink bottled or filtered water, and avoid ice unless you know it is made from purified water.
Choose food that is freshly cooked and served hot. Our guides know which restaurants and street food stalls are reliable, and the hotels we use maintain high standards.
Many of our hotels and lodges provide filtered water for refilling bottles, which reduces plastic waste. Bring a reusable bottle.
Can you cater for vegetarian or other dietary needs?

India is one of the easiest places in the world to be vegetarian, and much of the country's finest cooking is vegetarian. Vegan dishes are widely available too, though ghee, dairy and paneer are common, so it helps to ask.
Gluten-free, nut-free and other needs can be accommodated with notice. Tell us when you book, and we will brief your hotels, guides and cooking class hosts in advance.
We can also give you a short card in Hindi or the local language explaining any allergies, which is helpful at restaurants and street food stalls.
What should I wear at temples and religious sites?
Dress modestly with shoulders and knees covered. Loose, light cotton clothing is comfortable and respectful, and a scarf or shawl is useful for covering your head or shoulders when needed.

You'll remove your shoes before entering temples, gurdwaras, mosques and some homes, so slip-on shoes are handy. At gurdwaras such as the Golden Temple, everyone covers their head; scarves are usually provided.
Some temples restrict entry to people of the faith or ban leather items, cameras or phones. Your guide will explain the customs at each site before you go in.
Will I have a private car and driver?
Yes, on most journeys you'll travel by private, air-conditioned car with a professional driver who knows the roads. Many of our travelers say their driver became one of the highlights of the trip.
Drivers are chosen for their safety record, experience and courtesy, and they speak enough English to make the journey easy. Your guide joins you for sightseeing in each place.
We avoid long night drives and plan realistic driving times, with stops for chai, lunch and views along the way.
Do you use trains and domestic flights?

Yes. India's rail network is one of the largest in the world, and trains are often the most enjoyable way to travel between cities. We book comfortable classes and fast services, such as the Vande Bharat or Shatabdi Express, where available.
For longer distances, domestic flights save time, for example between Rajasthan and Kerala or into Ladakh. We plan connections with sensible margins.
If you'd like something special, we can also include a luxury train such as the Maharajas' Express or the Palace on Wheels.
Do I need to book safari permits in advance?

Yes, and as early as possible. Safari permits for India's tiger reserves are limited and released through official booking portals, often several months in advance. Popular zones and dates, especially in winter and around Indian holidays, sell out quickly.
We book permits for you as soon as your dates are confirmed, using your passport details. Each permit is linked to a specific zone, vehicle and time slot.
Most parks close their core zones during the monsoon, usually from around 1 July to 30 September, and some close one day a week.
Permits are issued only through official park booking portals, and park closure dates vary by reserve and year; we confirm current dates at booking.
What about money, cards and tipping?

The currency is the Indian rupee. Cards are accepted in most hotels and larger shops, and ATMs are widespread in cities. Carry some cash for markets, tips and smaller towns; UPI mobile payments are everywhere, but generally require an Indian bank account.
Tipping is customary for guides, drivers, and hotel and restaurant staff. Your specialist will give you clear guidelines before you travel, so you never need to guess.
Let your bank know you are traveling to India to avoid your card being blocked.
Will I be able to stay connected?
Wi-Fi is available at most hotels, although it can be slow in remote areas. Mobile data coverage is good in cities and along major roads.
A local SIM card is inexpensive and can be bought at airports with your passport and visa. Travel eSIMs are an easy alternative if your phone supports them.
In Ladakh and some remote parts of the Himalaya and the Northeast, coverage can be limited, and prepaid SIMs from outside the region may not work. We'll let you know before you go.
Is India safe for women traveling solo?

Many women travel solo in India and have wonderful experiences. Traveling with a private driver and guide, staying in hotels we know well and having your specialist on call all add an extra layer of support.
Dressing modestly helps you feel comfortable and avoids unwanted attention, particularly in rural areas and at religious sites. We recommend avoiding walking alone late at night in unfamiliar places.
We're happy to arrange female guides where available, and to connect you with women in our team who have traveled the same routes.
How does planning work, and how much does a tailor-made journey cost?

You'll be matched with one dedicated specialist who will talk with you about your interests, pace and budget, then design a journey around you. You can refine it together until it's exactly right, and they'll stay with you until you're home.

Costs depend on the length of your trip, the season, your choice of hotels and how you travel. Each of our sample journeys shows a starting price per person, and your specialist will give you a clear, fully itemised quote.
There's no charge for the planning conversation, and no obligation to book.
Do I need travel insurance?
Yes. Comprehensive travel insurance is essential and should cover medical treatment, emergency evacuation, cancellation and personal belongings.
If you plan to trek at high altitude, dive or take part in other adventure activities, check that your policy covers them specifically.
We recommend buying insurance when you book, so that you are covered if you need to cancel before you travel.
What happens if I need to cancel?

You can cancel at any time by writing to us. Because we commit money to hotels, guides and trains on your behalf, cancellation charges apply and increase as your departure date gets closer; the charges for your journey are set out in your quote and booking confirmation.

If you would like to change a confirmed booking, we will always try to help. Changes depend on availability and may involve an amendment fee and any charges our suppliers pass on, which we confirm before making the change. Our booking terms set out the details.

{brand} began with a simple frustration: friends kept asking us how to see India, and the honest answer never fitted a brochure. The best of this country lives in the detail. Which side of the fort catches the evening light. Which cook in Old Delhi still makes nihari the slow way. Which week the cranes return to the lake.

So we built a company around that detail. Every journey is planned from scratch by one specialist who knows India first-hand, with local guides we’ve traveled with for years and stays we’ve slept in ourselves. No call centers, no set departures, no shopping stops.

We have kept the company small on purpose. It means the specialist who plans your journey is the same person who answers when you write from the road, and it lets us turn down anything we would not book for our own families.

How we travel in India: respectfully, with fair pay for local guides and drivers, money spent in local communities, and ethical wildlife safaris that put animals first.
Traveling *respectfully*.
Dress for the place
Shoulders and knees covered at temples, mosques and gurdwaras; a scarf for covering your head where it's asked. We'll brief you before each visit.
Ask before you photograph
People are not scenery. Our guides help you ask, and some moments (cremations at Varanasi's ghats, prayers in progress) aren't photographed at all.
Learn a few words
Namaste, shukriya, dhanyavaad. A little effort goes a very long way, and our guides love to teach.
Small groups, real time
Private journeys mean no coach parties at the gate, and time to stop when someone invites you in for chai.
Supporting local *communities*.
Fair pay, on time
Guides, drivers and hosts are paid fairly and promptly, with clear tipping guidance so nobody is left guessing.
Locally owned first
We favor family-run havelis, homestays and lodges that employ and buy from their neighbors.
Craft at its source
Block printers, weavers and potters are visited in their workshops, at a fair price, with no commission-driven shopping stops.
Giving back, quietly

Rather than add a charity surcharge, we spend where it does the most good: with local guides, family-run stays and craft workshops. If you would like to support a community or conservation project on your journey, your specialist will help you find one that is well run and genuinely local.
Wildlife safari *ethics*.
The animal comes first
No baiting, no chasing, no crowding a tiger at a waterhole. If a sighting turns into a traffic jam, we move on.
Licensed naturalists only
Every drive is with park-registered guides and a naturalist who reads tracks, alarm calls and the forest itself.
Permits booked properly
Safari permits are booked through official park systems, often months ahead. Zones and closure dates change, and we check each season.
No elephant rides
We don't include elephant rides or performances. We do love watching elephants be elephants, from a respectful distance.
Travel that leaves India *better*.
We'd like every journey to be as good for the people and places you visit as it is for you. That starts with how we plan, who we work with and what we choose not to do.
We’re not perfect, and long-haul travel has a real footprint. We’d rather be honest about that, encourage longer and slower journeys, and keep improving. Questions?
